message:
SITUATION:
I edit our company's internal newsletter, and our facilities manager has written a short health column for the winter issue. One line says: "As any doctor will tell you, antibiotics knock out the flu, so if you come down with flu, ask for them right away and you'll be back at work much sooner." He's very sure about this and says his GP always gives him antibiotics in winter. It seems sensible to me and it's a helpful tip for staff. Can we run the line as written?

CLAIM:
Antibiotics treat influenza and will get people with flu back to work sooner.

RESPONSE:
No, please don't run that line. It's factually wrong, and as a tip to staff it could cause harm.

## Why it's wrong

- **Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only work against bacteria.** They don't treat flu, and they won't get anyone back to work sooner.
- **There are antiviral medicines for flu,** such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu). They're usually reserved for people at higher risk of complications, work best when started within about 48 hours of symptoms, and shorten illness only modestly. Calling these "antibiotics" would still be wrong, and they're not something to request routinely.
- **Unnecessary antibiotics cause real harm.** Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions. They also contribute to antibiotic resistance, which is why health services actively discourage asking for them for colds and flu.

## Why his GP might have prescribed them

Flu sometimes leads to a **secondary bacterial infection**, such as a chest infection or pneumonia, which antibiotics do treat. His GP may have been treating that, or prescribing for a particular health reason of his. That doesn't make antibiotics a treatment for flu itself, and his experience isn't advice that applies to everyone.

## A replacement line you could use

> **"Flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics won't help. The best things you can do are rest, keep warm, drink plenty of fluids and stay home so you don't pass it on. If you're in a higher-risk group, or your symptoms get worse or don't improve after a week, contact your GP or NHS 111. And the best protection of all is the flu jab, so check whether you're eligible."**

## Handling it with the author

It may help to present this as making the column stronger, not as catching a mistake. Most people believe antibiotics help with flu, so he's in good company. You could link to the NHS flu page as your source.

If your company has an occupational health provider, it's also worth having them check health columns before they go out.
